A 2022 meta-analysis (33 randomized trials) reported reduced postoperative pain after massage, but heterogeneity was extremely high, no trial was double-blind, and the real effect is uncertain. Massage after surgery is done only with the agreement of the medical team.

A 2024 meta-analysis of 39 randomized trials on acupressure (3,395 participants) reported reduced anxiety, but heterogeneity was very high (up to 100%), almost all trials had a risk of bias, and in comparisons with sham (placebo) acupressure the difference was not statistically significant. The authors acknowledge the low quality of the studies. The results suggest a possible relaxation effect, not firm evidence, and do not replace treatment for persistent anxiety.
Fatigue or heaviness
Tired eyes: brow ridge and middle of the eyebrow

The partner presses with both thumbs on both LR3, on the top of the foot, in the hollow where the bones of toes 1 and 2 meet. At the same time, you press LI4 on one hand with the thumb of the other, for 30 seconds, then switch hands for another 30 seconds (LR3 stay pressed the whole time). Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 4–6 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

The partner holds the occiput with one hand, with the thumb and middle finger on the two GB20, in a pincer across the nape. With the thumb of the other hand they press gently into the central hollow, GV16, below the occipital protuberance, upward and slightly forward. Pressure stays light to moderate (3–5/10). Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 3–5 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

The partner places the thumbs on BL23, on the muscles beside the spine at waist level, and on BL52, 3 cun lateral. They press simultaneously with light to moderate pressure (3–5/10), without pushing deep, 30–45 seconds on each side, only on the muscle beside the spine, with no strikes and no pressure on the flanks or ribs. They ask “how is the pressure?” every 15–20 seconds; at “stop” they stop immediately. Breathe slowly together. Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 4–6 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

The partner places a thumb on GB21, on the trapezius muscle, halfway between the nape and the tip of the shoulder, and presses slowly downward, into the muscle, without pushing deep toward the lung apex. With the thumb of the other hand they press simultaneously on SI11, in the hollow below the middle of the scapular spine, on the muscle (not with the elbow). You tell them when the pressure reaches 4–6/10 and breathe slowly. Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 4–6 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

The partner places a thumb on LI11, at the end of the elbow crease, and the other thumb on LI4, in the muscle between the thumb and index finger. They press simultaneously with medium pressure, hold 45–60 seconds while you breathe slowly, then switch arms. Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 4–6 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

The partner places a thumb on PC6, 2 finger-widths above the wrist crease, between the two tendons, and the other hand on ST36, below the kneecap, lateral to the tibia. They press simultaneously, with comfortable medium pressure (4–6/10; gentler on PC6), 60–90 seconds, while you breathe slowly. Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 4–6 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

The partner places one thumb on LU9, in the wrist crease on the thumb side, where the pulse can be felt, and the other on HT7, in the crease, on the little-finger side. They press simultaneously and lightly, without stopping the pulse, with comfortable medium pressure (4–6/10), and you both breathe slowly together. Before you begin, agree on a stop signal (“stop” or a raised hand). The person pressing asks “how is the pressure?” at the start and every 15–20 seconds (target: 4–6 out of 10); the person being pressed can ask for lighter, firmer or stopping at any time, without explanation.

On an abdominal or inguinal hernia, stoma, insulin pump or catheter do not press the area; with a pacemaker or other implanted device do not massage the area of the device and ask your doctor.
Directly on bones, on recent scars, on irritated skin, on inflamed or painful tendons.
On skin with infections (bacterial, fungal, viral), rashes, open wounds, burns, active eczema or other skin lesions: do not massage the affected area.
On the temples the pressure stays gentle (temporal artery). If the pain is new, throbbing, with vision disturbances or appeared after an injury, do not do acupressure and seek medical advice.
On severe varicose veins, phlebitis or ulcer areas: do not massage locally.
On inflamed, swollen, warm areas, with unexplained pain or strong sensitivity to touch.

Can relax the muscles and joints of the arms and legs and give a feeling of relief after exertion.
